vignette:
Arthur, a 73-year-old divorced journalist, still remembers the taste of smoke and burnt metal that filled his mouth as he stood among the wreckage of the collapsed convention center. He had arrived early to photograph the aftermath of the deliberately set explosion—a man-made disaster that killed 27 people—and the image he captured of a child’s shoe half-buried in debris won an award he can no longer bear to look at. Every time his phone buzzes with a news alert, his throat tightens. The buzz alone now makes him certain that he is permanently damaged and will never recover a normal life. When he scrolls past a photograph of any disaster—even a house fire in another state—the event replays in his mind like a film he cannot stop, and for a moment he feels the heat on his skin and hears the screams again, as if he is right there. The memory feels so extreme that he sometimes tells himself it could not have really happened to him, yet his body reacts as if it is happening now.

Arthur has come to believe that if he lets himself think about the explosion, he will completely lose control and never recover the ability to feel normal again. That certainty that he could not handle it kept pulling him back into the moment itself, as if his mind needed to test whether this time he would finally shatter, and the memory came sharper each time he told himself it was too dangerous. This belief has hollowed out his days; nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore, and he spends impulsively on new cameras, lenses, and online subscriptions—anything to distract from the gap where purpose used to be. That compulsive spending, however, often leads him back to the exact photos he was trying to avoid, because his credit card statements remind him of the equipment he used that day. He now sits only with his back to the wall in restaurants and coffee shops, scanning every face that enters. Yet this scanning only makes him feel more endangered, as though his constant watchfulness proves that danger is lurking. He listens for sounds that might mean someone is forcing his apartment door, even though he lives on the fifteenth floor. In any room he notices potential weapons—a letter opener, a fire extinguisher, a heavy ashtray—and he cannot relax even when he knows he is safe. Because he feels so unsafe, everyday noises like a car backfiring or a neighbor’s door slamming now hit him like the sounds of the disaster itself. Feeling this hunted all the time had become the most convincing evidence he had that his life was permanently broken, that the person he used to be was gone for good. This hunted feeling itself often pulls him straight back to the explosion, as if his body remembers the fear before his mind does.

When an unfamiliar taste touches his tongue—something metallic, or the acrid tang of burnt wiring—Arthur’s mind snaps back to the explosion site, and the unreality of the memory deepens: he freezes completely where he stands, unable to move or speak until the taste fades. After one of those episodes, Arthur would find himself noticing every unusual smell in his apartment—burnt toast, bleach, a neighbor’s cooking oil—as though the world had become covered in clues he could not afford to miss. He is aware that this freezing only makes the memory more vivid when it returns, because the fear of the next unpredictable trigger becomes a constant hum in his body. He monitors for any sound that might signal an intruder, and his hypervigilance often leads him to re-experience the disaster, because his racing heart and scanning eyes mirror the panic he felt that day. His compulsive spending, too, has a way of circling back: after buying something he does not need, he feels a brief relief that quickly dissolves into shame, and the shame reinforces his conviction that he will never feel normal emotions again. That belief, in turn, makes it harder for him to sit with the memory, so he avoids it more intensely, and the avoidance only confirms that the memory is too dangerous to face.

Arthur has stopped accepting assignments that involve unpredictable locations or crowds. He works from home now, filing stories by email, but even there, the taste of his morning coffee sometimes carries an echo of smoke, and he finds himself checking his window locks three times before he can concentrate. His ex-wife stopped calling years ago; his children send texts he rarely answers. What finally brought him to the clinic was a week during which he could not leave his apartment because every time he stepped outside, a car backfired or a siren wailed, and he felt the pavement shake beneath him. He is terrified that his mind is slipping away, but what he hopes—though he can barely admit it—is that someone can convince him the memory is real, and that he can survive it.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals influence or trigger the memory.
No paragraph conveys that the memory causes the patient to perceive or encounter triggers.
No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat leads to negative appraisals.
No paragraph conveys that the perceived threat causes triggers to appear or be noticed.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals influence or trigger the memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the memory causes the patient to perceive or encounter triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the perceived threat causes triggers to appear or be noticed.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

violations.explanation: Triggers -> Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that a triggering stimulus directly causes negative appraisals; the causal path always goes through memory first.
Threat -> Memory: No paragraph shows that a sense of threat directly brings on the trauma memory; the memory is triggered by cues or by maladaptive strategies, not by threat itself.
Threat -> Triggers: No paragraph indicates that the patient's sense of threat directly creates or amplifies triggering stimuli; hypervigilance is a maladaptive strategy that mediates this.

Maladaptive Strategies -> Threat: No paragraph describes the patient's maladaptive behaviours (e.g., avoidance, compulsive spending, hypervigilance) as increasing his sense of threat; instead, threat drives these strategies.
